claim: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) are key enzymes in DNA metabolism.
source: Ribonucleotide reductases (RNRs) are key enzymes in DNA metabolism, with allosteric mechanisms controlling substrate specificity and overall activity.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the manuscript's introduction and references to prior work.

claim: In RNRs, the ATP-cone has been found exclusively in the catalytic subunit.
source: In RNRs, the activity master-switch, the ATP-cone, has been found exclusively in the catalytic subunit.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge prior to the current study's findings.

claim: ATP-cones were discovered in the radical-generating subunit of two class I RNR subclasses whose catalytic subunit lacks the ATP-cone.
source: In two class I RNR subclasses whose catalytic subunit lacks the ATP-cone, we discovered ATP-cones in the radical-generating subunit.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by phylogenetic analysis and sequence data.

claim: The ATP-cone in the Leeuwenhoekiella blandensis radical-generating subunit regulates activity via quaternary structure induced by binding of nucleotides.
source: The ATP-cone in the Leeuwenhoekiella blandensis radical-generating subunit regulates activity via quaternary structure induced by binding of nucleotides.
evidence: This is supported by GEMMA and SEC experiments showing nucleotide-dependent oligomerization.

claim: ATP induces enzymatically competent dimers of L. blandensis NrdB.
source: ATP induces enzymatically competent dimers, whereas dATP induces non-productive tetramers, resulting in different holoenzymes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC and GEMMA experiments showing ATP-induced dimer formation.

claim: dATP induces non-productive tetramers of L. blandensis NrdB.
source: ATP induces enzymatically competent dimers, whereas dATP induces non-productive tetramers, resulting in different holoenzymes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA, SEC, and activity assays showing dATP-induced tetramer formation and enzyme inhibition.

claim: The NrdB tetramer forms by interactions between ATP-cones.
source: The tetramer forms by interactions between ATP-cones, shown by a 2.45 Å crystal structure.
evidence: This is directly observed in the crystal structure (PDB 5OLK).

claim: The crystal structure of L. blandensis NrdB was determined at 2.45 Å resolution.
source: The tetramer forms by interactions between ATP-cones, shown by a 2.45 Å crystal structure.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and detailed in the results with crystallographic data.

claim: L. blandensis NrdB contains an MnIIIMnIV metal center.
source: We also present evidence for an MnIIIMnIV metal center.
evidence: This is supported by EPR spectroscopy showing a multiline signal characteristic of MnIIIMnIV.

claim: This represents the first observation of transfer of an allosteric domain between components of the same enzyme complex.
source: To our knowledge, this represents the first observation of transfer of an allosteric domain between components of the same enzyme complex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the phylogenetic and structural analysis presented in the study.

claim: RNRs provide the only known de novo pathway for the biosynthesis of deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs).
source: RNRs are essential enzymes in all free-living cells, providing the only known de novo pathway for the biosynthesis of deoxyribonucleotides (dNTPs), the immediate precursors for DNA synthesis and repair (Hofer et al., 2012; Nordlund and Reichard, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Imbalanced levels of dNTPs lead to increased mutation rates.
source: To avoid imbalanced levels of dNTPs and the increased mutation rates that are the inevitable consequences of this (Kumar et al., 2011; Mathews, 2006; Watt et al., 2016), RNRs are tightly controlled through transcriptional and allosteric regulation, subcellular compartmentalization and small protein inhibitors (Pai and Kearsey, 2017; Torrents, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The ATP-cone acts as a regulatory master switch that senses intracellular nucleotide concentrations by competitive binding of ATP and dATP.
source: Acting as a regulatory master switch, the a-site senses intracellular nucleotide concentrations by competitive binding of ATP and dATP. In the presence of ATP the enzyme is active, and when concentrations of dNTPs rise, binding of dATP switches the enzyme off.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ATP-cone function, supported by prior studies.

claim: The ATP-cone domain has been observed exclusively at the N-terminus of the catalytic subunit NrdA (class I), NrdJ (class II) and NrdD (class III) prior to this study.
source: Although regulation has been lost and gained repeatedly in RNRs through evolutionary time, to date, the ATP-cone domain has been observed exclusively at the N-terminus of the catalytic subunit NrdA (class I), NrdJ (class II) and NrdD (class III).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge before the current discovery.

claim: Three phylogenetically well-supported subclasses of class I RNR never have ATP-cones in the catalytic subunit: NrdE, NrdAi and NrdAk.
source: A recent phylogenetic subclassification of RNRs reveals that three phylogenetically well-supported subclasses of class I never have ATP-cones (Jonna et al., 2015) (http://rnrdb.pfitmap.org): NrdE, NrdAi and NrdAk.
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis cited from prior work.

claim: ATP-cones were discovered attached to the radical-generating subunit in two RNR subclasses: NrdF (the Ib subclass) and NrdBi.
source: In two of these subclasses we instead discovered ATP-cones attached to their corresponding radical-generating subunit: NrdF (the Ib subclass) and NrdBi.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by sequence analysis and phylogenetic data.

claim: When dATP is bound at the a-site, high molecular mass oligomers are formed in which the radical transfer pathway is distorted.
source: Crystal structures, cryo-electron microscopy reconstructions and small-angle X-ray scattering studies of inhibited complexes have revealed that when dATP is bound at the a-site, high molecular mass oligomers are formed, in which the radical transfer pathway is distorted (Ando et al., 2011; Ando et al., 2016; Fairman et al., 2011; Johansson et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: In E. coli RNR, the active NrdAB complex is α2β2.
source: In Escherichia coli RNR, the active NrdAB complex is α2β2, whereas the inactive form is an α4β4 ring-shaped octamer where the ATP-cones in the α subunits sequester the β subunits in a non-productive conformation (Ando et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies of E. coli RNR.

claim: In E. coli RNR, the inactive form is an α4β4 ring-shaped octamer.
source: In Escherichia coli RNR, the active NrdAB complex is α2β2, whereas the inactive form is an α4β4 ring-shaped octamer where the ATP-cones in the α subunits sequester the β subunits in a non-productive conformation (Ando et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: In eukaryotic class I RNR, the inactive complex has an α6 stoichiometry.
source: In the eukaryotic class I RNR, the inactive complex differs from the one in E. coli in that it has an α6 stoichiometry.
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior structural studies.

claim: L. blandensis was isolated from Mediterranean surface seawater.
source: L. blandensis was isolated from Mediterranean surface seawater and belongs to Flavobacteriaceae, the major family of marine Bacteroidetes, with important roles in carbon flow and nutrient turnover in the sea during and following algal blooms (Fernández-Gómez et al., 2013; Pinhassi et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as background information with citation support.

claim: L. blandensis possesses two RNRs: a class II without ATP-cone, and the class I NrdAi/NrdBi.
source: L. blandensis possesses two RNRs: a class II without ATP-cone, and the class I NrdAi/NrdBi, which lacks an ATP-cone in NrdA and instead contains an ATP-cone positioned at the N-terminus of NrdB.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of L. blandensis.

claim: At high dATP concentrations, inhibited higher oligomeric complexes of the L. blandensis NrdAi/NrdBi holoenzyme are favoured.
source: Superficially, the allosteric mechanism of L. blandensis NrdAi/NrdBi holoenzyme is similar to when the ATP-cone is contained in the catalytic subunit. At high dATP concentrations, inhibited higher oligomeric complexes of the holoenzyme are favoured.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA and SEC experiments showing dATP-induced oligomerization.

claim: In the L. blandensis class I RNR, the oligomerization is driven by a shift towards tetramers of the radical-generating subunit.
source: However, in the L. blandensis class I RNR, the oligomerization is driven by a shift towards tetramers of the radical-generating subunit.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA and SEC experiments showing NrdB tetramer formation.

claim: Ninety-three sequences in NCBI's RefSeq database are NrdBi proteins with N-terminally positioned ATP-cones.
source: Ninety-three sequences in NCBI's RefSeq database are NrdBi proteins with N-terminally positioned ATP-cones.
evidence: This is based on database searches and sequence analysis.

claim: NrdBi proteins with ATP-cones are encoded by viruses and bacteria from several phyla, although the Flavobacteriales order in the Bacteroidetes phylum predominate (70 sequences).
source: They are encoded by viruses and bacteria from several phyla, although the Flavobacteriales order in the Bacteroidetes phylum predominate (70 sequences, http://rnrdb.pfitmap.org).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic distribution analysis of sequences.

claim: NrdF proteins with a C-terminally positioned ATP-cone are only encoded by a few species of the Meiothermus genus of the Deinococcus-Thermus phylum.
source: NrdF proteins with a C-terminally positioned ATP-cone are only encoded by a few species of the Meiothermus genus of the Deinococcus-Thermus phylum (http://rnrdb.pfitmap.org).
evidence: This is based on sequence database analysis.

claim: All species encoding NrdB proteins with ATP-cones in their genomes also encode other RNRs.
source: All species encoding NrdB proteins with ATP-cones in their genomes also encode other RNRs.
evidence: This is based on genomic analysis of organisms with NrdB-ATP-cone proteins.

claim: L. blandensis RNR has a similar specificity regulation pattern to most characterized RNRs.
source: Using a four-substrate activity assay in the presence of saturating concentrations of the s-site effectors dTTP, dGTP or ATP, we found that L. blandensis RNR has a similar specificity regulation pattern to most characterized RNRs (Hofer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays with different substrates and effectors.

claim: ATP stimulated the reduction of CDP and UDP in L. blandensis RNR.
source: ATP stimulated the reduction of CDP and UDP, whereas dTTP stimulated the reduction of GDP, and dGTP stimulated the reduction of ADP and GDP (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 activity assay data.

claim: dTTP stimulated the reduction of GDP in L. blandensis RNR.
source: ATP stimulated the reduction of CDP and UDP, whereas dTTP stimulated the reduction of GDP, and dGTP stimulated the reduction of ADP and GDP (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 activity assay data.

claim: dGTP stimulated the reduction of ADP and GDP in L. blandensis RNR.
source: ATP stimulated the reduction of CDP and UDP, whereas dTTP stimulated the reduction of GDP, and dGTP stimulated the reduction of ADP and GDP (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 activity assay data.

claim: L. blandensis RNR was completely inactive in the absence of allosteric effectors.
source: The enzyme was completely inactive in the absence of allosteric effectors.
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays shown in Figure 2.

claim: dTTP-induced GDP reduction dramatically increased in the presence of ATP in L. blandensis RNR.
source: Using mixtures of allosteric effectors, we observed that dTTP-induced GDP reduction dramatically increased in the presence of ATP (Figure 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2 activity assay data.

claim: The presence of ATP activated L. blandensis RNR.
source: The presence of ATP clearly activated the enzyme (Figure 3a), while dATP activated the enzyme when used at low concentrations and was inhibitory at 30 µM and higher (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 3a.

claim: dATP activated L. blandensis RNR at low concentrations and was inhibitory at 30 µM and higher.
source: The presence of ATP clearly activated the enzyme (Figure 3a), while dATP activated the enzyme when used at low concentrations and was inhibitory at 30 µM and higher (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 3b.

claim: The ATP-cone deletion mutant NrdB∆99 reached a lower maximum activity compared to the wild type enzyme.
source: An ATP-cone deletion mutant NrdB∆99, lacking the N-terminal 99 residues, reached a lower maximum activity compared to the wild type enzyme, suggesting that it was not activated by ATP beyond saturation of the s-site in the NrdA, nor was it inhibited by dATP (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays comparing wild type and mutant in Figure 3a-b.

claim: NrdB∆99 was not activated by ATP beyond saturation of the s-site in NrdA.
source: An ATP-cone deletion mutant NrdB∆99, lacking the N-terminal 99 residues, reached a lower maximum activity compared to the wild type enzyme, suggesting that it was not activated by ATP beyond saturation of the s-site in the NrdA, nor was it inhibited by dATP (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 3a-b.

claim: NrdB∆99 was not inhibited by dATP.
source: An ATP-cone deletion mutant NrdB∆99, lacking the N-terminal 99 residues, reached a lower maximum activity compared to the wild type enzyme, suggesting that it was not activated by ATP beyond saturation of the s-site in the NrdA, nor was it inhibited by dATP (Figure 3a–b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 3a-b.

claim: The KL value for ATP binding to the s-site in NrdA is 30 μM.
source: From the NrdB∆99 effector titrations, we could calculate KL values – the concentrations of allosteric effectors that give half maximal enzyme activity – for binding of ATP and dATP to the s-site in NrdA to 30 and 1.4 μM respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from activity assay data with NrdB∆99.

claim: The KL value for dATP binding to the s-site in NrdA is 1.4 μM.
source: From the NrdB∆99 effector titrations, we could calculate KL values – the concentrations of allosteric effectors that give half maximal enzyme activity – for binding of ATP and dATP to the s-site in NrdA to 30 and 1.4 μM respectively.
evidence: This is calculated from activity assay data with NrdB∆99.

claim: ATP activates wild type NrdB through the a-site with a KL of 96 μM.
source: Titration of ATP into wild type NrdB in the presence of an excess of NrdA saturated with dTTP showed that it activates the enzyme through the a-site with a KL of 96 μM (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is calculated from activity assay data in Figure 3c.

claim: The Ki value for dATP binding to the a-site is 20 µM in the presence of s-site saturating dTTP concentration.
source: For the corresponding inhibition by dATP binding to the a-site, we calculated the Ki value - the binding constant of a non-competitive inhibitor - to be 20 µM in the presence of an s-site saturating dTTP concentration (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is calculated from activity assay data in Figure 3d.

claim: dADP interacts with the a-site in the presence of s-site saturating dTTP concentrations.
source: In addition to ATP and dATP, dADP was also found to interact, whereas ADP, AMP and dAMP had no effect (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 3e.

claim: ADP, AMP and dAMP had no effect on the a-site in the presence of s-site saturating dTTP.
source: In addition to ATP and dATP, dADP was also found to interact, whereas ADP, AMP and dAMP had no effect (Figure 3e).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 3e.

claim: dADP inhibited L. blandensis RNR enzyme activity, although less strongly than dATP.
source: Titration with dADP inhibited the enzyme activity, although less strongly than dATP (Figure 3f).
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 3f.

claim: In the absence of allosteric effectors, NrdB is mainly monomeric at low protein concentrations suitable for GEMMA analyses.
source: In the absence of allosteric effectors, NrdB (β) is mainly monomeric (theoretically 51.8 kDa) and, in contrast to most studied NrdB proteins, it does not readily form dimers at the low protein concentration range suitable for GEMMA analyses (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4a.

claim: Addition of dATP (50 μM) dramatically shifted the equilibrium of NrdB towards tetramers.
source: Addition of dATP (50 μM) dramatically shifted the equilibrium towards tetramers β4, which became the major form under these conditions (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4a.

claim: NrdB tetramers reached their half-maximum mass concentration at around 10 µM dATP.
source: Titration of increasing concentrations of dATP to NrdB showed that the tetramers reached their half-maximum mass concentration at around 10 µM dATP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA titration experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of 50 μM dADP induced formation of NrdB tetramers, although less efficiently than with dATP.
source: Addition of 50 μM dADP also induced formation of NrdB tetramers, although less efficiently than with dATP (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4a.

claim: The NrdB∆99 mutant was mainly monomeric regardless if dATP was present or not.
source: In contrast, the NrdB∆99 mutant, lacking the ATP-cone (Figure 4b), was mainly monomeric regardless if dATP was present or not (Figure 4b), demonstrating that the NrdB-linked ATP-cone is required for dATP-induced tetramer formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4b.

claim: The NrdB-linked ATP-cone is required for dATP-induced tetramer formation.
source: In contrast, the NrdB∆99 mutant, lacking the ATP-cone (Figure 4b), was mainly monomeric regardless if dATP was present or not (Figure 4b), demonstrating that the NrdB-linked ATP-cone is required for dATP-induced tetramer formation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing wild type and mutant NrdB in GEMMA experiments.

claim: NrdA was a monomer in the absence of allosteric effectors.
source: NrdA was a monomer (theoretically 70.6 kDa) in the absence of allosteric effectors, while addition of dATP prompted formation of dimers (Figure 4c)
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4c.

claim: Addition of dATP prompted formation of NrdA dimers.
source: NrdA was a monomer (theoretically 70.6 kDa) in the absence of allosteric effectors, while addition of dATP prompted formation of dimers (Figure 4c)
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4c.

claim: A mixture of NrdA and NrdB in the presence of 100 µM dATP formed a large complex of 340 kDa with the expected mass of an α2β4 complex.
source: To assess the oligomeric state of the complete enzymatic complex of the inactive L. blandensis RNR, a mixture of NrdA (α) and NrdB (β) in the presence of 100 µM dATP was analyzed with GEMMA (Figure 4c). The two subunits formed a large complex of 340 kDa with the expected mass of an α2β4 complex (theoretically 348 kDa), and at higher protein concentration a complex of 465 kDa with the expected mass of an α4β4 complex (theoretically 488 kDa) started to appear.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4c.

claim: At higher protein concentration, a complex of 465 kDa with the expected mass of an α4β4 complex started to appear.
source: The two subunits formed a large complex of 340 kDa with the expected mass of an α2β4 complex (theoretically 348 kDa), and at higher protein concentration a complex of 465 kDa with the expected mass of an α4β4 complex (theoretically 488 kDa) started to appear.
evidence: This is demonstrated by GEMMA analysis in Figure 4c.

claim: NrdB was in a monomer-dimer-tetramer equilibrium in SEC experiments.
source: The SEC experiments showed that NrdB was in a monomer-dimer-tetramer equilibrium (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a) with an average size comparable to dimers (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: ATP and dATP promoted the equilibrium of NrdB to shift to dimers and tetramers, respectively.
source: Similar to the results with GEMMA, it was mainly a monomer at lower protein concentrations (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a). ATP and dATP promoted the equilibrium to shift to dimers and tetramers, respectively (Figure 5a, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Without effectors, NrdA was mainly in a monomeric state.
source: Without effectors, NrdA was mainly in a monomeric state, while it was dominated by dimers in the presence of either of the two effectors (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments in Figure 5b.

claim: NrdA was dominated by dimers in the presence of either ATP or dATP.
source: Without effectors, NrdA was mainly in a monomeric state, while it was dominated by dimers in the presence of either of the two effectors (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments in Figure 5b.

claim: When NrdA and NrdB were mixed in the absence of allosteric effectors, no complex was visible by SEC.
source: When NrdA and NrdB were mixed in the absence of allosteric effectors, no complex was visible. After addition of ATP, a new complex of ~200 kDa appeared (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments in Figure 5c.

claim: After addition of ATP, a new complex of ~200 kDa appeared in mixtures of NrdA and NrdB.
source: When NrdA and NrdB were mixed in the absence of allosteric effectors, no complex was visible. After addition of ATP, a new complex of ~200 kDa appeared (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments in Figure 5c.

claim: The ~200 kDa complex formed in the presence of ATP contains both NrdA and NrdB in a 1:1 molar ratio.
source: To verify its composition and stoichiometry, we analyzed fractions eluted from SEC on SDS PAGE. Both NrdA and NrdB were visible on the gel in a 1:1 molar ratio (Figure 5c insert).
evidence: This is demonstrated by SDS PAGE analysis of SEC fractions in Figure 5c insert.

claim: The complex formed in conditions promoting active RNR is conceivably an α2β2 complex.
source: This complex, formed in conditions promoting active RNR, is conceivably an α2β2 complex.
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular mass and stoichiometry data from SEC and SDS PAGE.

claim: After addition of dATP, a complex with a molecular mass consistent with α4β4 eluted from SEC.
source: After addition of the inhibiting effector dATP, a complex with a molecular mass consistent with α4β4 eluted.
evidence: This is demonstrated by SEC experiments in Figure 5c.

claim: The crystal structure of L. blandensis NrdB at 2.45 Å resolution revealed a novel tetrameric arrangement hitherto not observed in the RNR family.
source: The crystal structure of the dATP-inhibited complex of L. blandensis NrdB at 2.45 Å resolution (PDB 5OLK) revealed a novel tetrameric arrangement hitherto not observed in the RNR family, with approximate 222 point symmetry (Figure 6a, Table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the crystal structure (PDB 5OLK) shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Each NrdB monomer consists of an ATP-cone domain (residues 1–103) joined by a short linker (104-106) to a metal-binding α-helical core domain (residues 107–398) and a disordered C-terminus (399-427).
source: Each monomer consists of an ATP-cone domain (residues 1–103) joined by a short linker (104-106) to a metal-binding α-helical core domain (residues 107–398) and a disordered C-terminus (399-427).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The NrdB dimer buries about 1100 Å2 of solvent accessible area on each monomer.
source: The dimer buries about 1100 Å2 of solvent accessible area on each monomer.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The tetrameric arrangement of NrdB is completely dependent on interactions between the ATP cone domains.
source: The tetrameric arrangement is completely dependent on interactions between the ATP cone domains, as no contacts are made between the core domains in the two dimers that make up the tetramer (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6a.

claim: No contacts are made between the core domains in the two dimers that make up the NrdB tetramer.
source: The tetrameric arrangement is completely dependent on interactions between the ATP cone domains, as no contacts are made between the core domains in the two dimers that make up the tetramer (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6a.

claim: The ATP-cone domain in L. blandensis NrdB is structurally very similar to the one recently identified in the NrdA protein of P. aeruginosa.
source: The ATP-cone domain in L. blandensis NrdB is structurally very similar to the one recently identified in the NrdA protein of P. aeruginosa (Johansson et al., 2016). The root-mean-square deviation for 92 equivalent Cα atoms is 1.2 Å.
evidence: This is demonstrated by structural comparison with RMSD calculation.

claim: The root-mean-square deviation for 92 equivalent Cα atoms between L. blandensis NrdB and P. aeruginosa NrdA ATP-cones is 1.2 Å.
source: The root-mean-square deviation for 92 equivalent Cα atoms is 1.2 Å.
evidence: This is calculated from structural comparison.

claim: The L. blandensis ATP-cone can bind two molecules of dATP.
source: The electron density unambiguously confirms the L. blandensis ATP-cone's ability to bind two molecules of dATP, which it shares with P. aeruginosa NrdA (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure electron density shown in Figure 6c.

claim: All amino acids involved in binding both dATP molecules in L. blandensis NrdB are conserved compared to P. aeruginosa NrdA, despite a local sequence identity of only 31%.
source: Despite a local sequence identity of only 31% to P. aeruginosa NrdA, all amino acids involved in binding both dATP molecules are conserved (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal structures and sequences.

claim: The two dATP molecules bind in a 'tail-to-tail' arrangement that orients the base of the 'non-canonical' dATP towards the fourth, most C-terminal helix.
source: The two dATP molecules bind in a 'tail-to-tail' arrangement that orients the base of the 'non-canonical' dATP towards the fourth, most C-terminal helix, an arrangement made possible by the binding of a Mg2+ ion between the triphosphate moieties.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: A Mg2+ ion binds between the triphosphate moieties of the two dATP molecules.
source: The two dATP molecules bind in a 'tail-to-tail' arrangement that orients the base of the 'non-canonical' dATP towards the fourth, most C-terminal helix, an arrangement made possible by the binding of a Mg2+ ion between the triphosphate moieties.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The interactions between the ATP-cones in L. blandensis NrdB are very similar to those seen in P. aeruginosa NrdA.
source: Remarkably, the interactions between the ATP-cones in L. blandensis NrdB are also very similar to those seen in P. aeruginosa NrdA (Johansson et al., 2016), despite the fact that the ATP-cone is attached to a structurally completely different core domain.
evidence: This is observed by comparing the crystal structures.

claim: The main interactions between ATP-cones occur between the last two helices α3 and α4 in respective ATP-cones.
source: The main interactions occur between the last two helices α3 and α4 in respective ATP-cones (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6d.

claim: A hydrophobic core in L. blandensis NrdB involving residues Met80, Ile92 and Ile93 in both monomers is reinforced by salt bridges between residues Asp73, Asp76 in one monomer and Lys89 in the other.
source: A hydrophobic core in L. blandensis NrdB involving residues Met80, Ile92 and Ile93 in both monomers is reinforced by salt bridges between residues Asp73, Asp76 in one monomer and Lys89 in the other.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The two ATP-cone domains bury ~510 Å2 of solvent accessible area.
source: The two domains bury ~510 Å2 of solvent accessible area.
evidence: This is calculated from the crystal structure.

claim: The ATP-cone interaction in L. blandensis NrdB buries slightly less area (~510 Å2) than the equivalent interaction in P. aeruginosa NrdA (~640 Å2).
source: This is slightly less than the ~640 Å2 buried in the equivalent interaction involving the ATP-cones of P. aeruginosa NrdA.
evidence: This is calculated by comparing the crystal structures.

claim: The dATP-induced tetramer leaves free the surfaces of both dimers of L. blandensis NrdB that are thought to interact with the NrdA subunit in productive RNR complexes.
source: Interestingly, the dATP-induced tetramer leaves free the surfaces of both dimers of L. blandensis NrdB that are thought to interact with the NrdA subunit in productive RNR complexes, which implies that one or two dimers of L. blandensis NrdA could attach to these surfaces in a near-productive fashion in α2β4 or α4β4 complexes (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6a.

claim: One or two dimers of L. blandensis NrdA could attach to the NrdB tetramer surfaces in a near-productive fashion in α2β4 or α4β4 complexes.
source: Interestingly, the dATP-induced tetramer leaves free the surfaces of both dimers of L. blandensis NrdB that are thought to interact with the NrdA subunit in productive RNR complexes, which implies that one or two dimers of L. blandensis NrdA could attach to these surfaces in a near-productive fashion in α2β4 or α4β4 complexes (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is inferred from the crystal structure and GEMMA/SEC data.

claim: Two metal ions bind to each of the monomers of L. blandensis NrdB.
source: Two metal ions are found to bind to each of the monomers of L. blandensis NrdB.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: The distance between metal ions in L. blandensis NrdB varies between 3.4–3.8 Å in the four monomers.
source: The distance between metal ions varies between 3.4–3.8 Å in the four monomers (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), but the metal coordination is very similar.
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structure shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The coordination distances in the L. blandensis NrdB metal center are long for an RNR metal center, with the shortest distances being 2.3–2.4 Å.
source: The coordination distances are long for an RNR metal center, with the shortest distances being 2.3–2.4 Å, in contrast to the more typical 1.9–2.1 Å seen in other NrdB proteins containing Mn or Fe.
evidence: This is measured from the crystal structure.

claim: Anomalous diffraction at three wavelengths was used to determine the nature of the metal in L. blandensis NrdB.
source: Anomalous diffraction at three wavelengths was used to determine the nature of the metal.
evidence: This is described in the methods and results.

claim: The metal site in the crystal is occupied by Ca2+ from the crystallization medium.
source: Figure 6—source data 1 shows that there is little difference in the peak heights at the metal ion positions in anomalous difference maps irrespective of wavelength, which strongly suggests that the metal site is occupied by Ca2+ from the crystallization medium.
evidence: This is demonstrated by anomalous diffraction data in Figure 6—source data 1.

claim: The presence of Ca2+ in the crystal is consistent with the long coordination distances observed.
source: The presence of Ca2+ is also consistent with the long coordination distances.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the observed coordination distances with expected values for different metals.

claim: An X-ray fluorescence spectrum of the crystal revealed only traces of Mn or Fe.
source: Furthermore, an X-ray fluorescence spectrum of the crystal (not shown) revealed only traces of Mn or Fe.
evidence: This is stated as experimental observation.

claim: Tyr207 is found near the metal site at the position expected for a radical-carrying Tyr.
source: Interestingly, Tyr207 is found near the metal site at the position expected for a radical-carrying Tyr, but it is not hydrogen-bonded to the metal site, its hydroxyl group being at around 6 Å from the side chain of Glu170.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Tyr207 is not hydrogen-bonded to the metal site in L. blandensis NrdB.
source: Interestingly, Tyr207 is found near the metal site at the position expected for a radical-carrying Tyr, but it is not hydrogen-bonded to the metal site, its hydroxyl group being at around 6 Å from the side chain of Glu170.
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure.

claim: Trp177 is completely conserved in the NrdBi subclass.
source: This tryptophan is completely conserved in the NrdBi subclass (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The first helix of the 4-helix bundle containing the metal center ligands has a very unusual distortion in the middle.
source: The first helix of the bundle has a very unusual distortion in the middle (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: In L. blandensis NrdB, residues 171–175 form a loop that bulges away from the metal site.
source: Normally this is an undistorted α-helix, but in L. blandensis NrdB, residues 171–175 form a loop that bulges away from the metal site, with the exception of Lys174, whose side chain is projected towards the metal site and is H-bonded to Glu170 (Figure 6e).
evidence: This is observed in the crystal structure shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The distortion in the first helix is not caused by the coordination of Ca2+ instead of the native metal.
source: However we are certain that the distortion is not caused by the coordination of Ca2+ instead of the native metal, as the structure is the same in crystals of the N-terminally truncated form grown in the presence of Mn2+, which will be presented elsewhere.
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with another crystal structure.

claim: X-band EPR spectroscopy of catalytically active samples revealed a mixture of signals from low and high-valent manganese species.
source: The nature of the native metallo-cofactor was addressed by X-band EPR spectroscopy and catalytically active samples were analyzed at 5–32 K. The spectra revealed a mixture of signals from low and high-valent manganese species (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EPR spectroscopy data in Figure 7a.

claim: At 5 K, a 6-line signal attributable to low valent Mn (MnII) was clearly visible in EPR spectra.
source: In particular, at 5 K a 6-line signal attributable to low valent Mn (MnII) was clearly visible, overlaid with a complex multiline signal with a width of approximately 1250G.
evidence: This is observed in EPR spectra shown in Figure 7a.

claim: A complex multiline signal with a width of approximately 1250G was observed in EPR spectra at 5 K.
source: In particular, at 5 K a 6-line signal attributable to low valent Mn (MnII) was clearly visible, overlaid with a complex multiline signal with a width of approximately 1250G.
evidence: This is observed in EPR spectra shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Increasing the temperature to 32 K resulted in a significant decrease of the multiline signal, while the 6-line feature remained relatively intense.
source: Increasing the temperature to 32 K resulted in a significant decrease of the latter signal, while the 6-line feature remained relatively intense (Figure 7a, top and middle).
evidence: This is observed in EPR spectra shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The shape, width and temperature dependence of the multiline signal are attributable to a strongly coupled MnIIIMnIV dimer (STotal = ½).
source: The shape, width and temperature dependence of the multiline signal are all highly reminiscent of the signal reported for super-oxidized manganese catalase as well as the 16-line signal observed during the assembly of the dimanganese/tyrosyl radical cofactor in NrdF RNR, and are attributable to a strongly coupled MnIIIMnIV dimer (STotal = ½) (Figure 7a, bottom) (Cotruvo et al., 2013; Zheng et al., 1994).
evidence: This is inferred by comparison with known EPR signatures of MnIIIMnIV dimers from cited literature.

claim: The low valent Mn species appeared to be weakly bound to the protein.
source: The low valent species appeared to be weakly bound to the protein, while the MnIIIMnIV dimer was retained in the protein following desalting (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EPR spectra before and after desalting in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The MnIIIMnIV dimer was retained in the protein following desalting.
source: The low valent species appeared to be weakly bound to the protein, while the MnIIIMnIV dimer was retained in the protein following desalting (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by EPR spectra before and after desalting in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observation of a high-valent Mn cofactor is consistent with the Mn-dependent increase in catalytic activity of the enzyme.
source: The observation of a high-valent Mn cofactor is consistent with the Mn-dependent increase in catalytic activity of the enzyme and its inhibition by the addition of Fe2+(Figure 7b–c), and is suggestive of a novel high-valent homodimeric Mn-cofactor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays with different metals in Figure 7b-c.

claim: Addition of Fe2+ inhibits the catalytic activity of L. blandensis RNR.
source: The observation of a high-valent Mn cofactor is consistent with the Mn-dependent increase in catalytic activity of the enzyme and its inhibition by the addition of Fe2+(Figure 7b–c), and is suggestive of a novel high-valent homodimeric Mn-cofactor.
evidence: This is demonstrated by activity assays in Figure 7c.

claim: The observation of a high-valent Mn cofactor is suggestive of a novel high-valent homodimeric Mn-cofactor.
source: The observation of a high-valent Mn cofactor is consistent with the Mn-dependent increase in catalytic activity of the enzyme and its inhibition by the addition of Fe2+(Figure 7b–c), and is suggestive of a novel high-valent homodimeric Mn-cofactor.
evidence: This is inferred from EPR and activity data.

claim: Earlier calculations have shown that high-valent Mn-dimers have reduction potentials similar to that of the tyrosyl radical in standard class I RNRs.
source: Indeed, earlier calculations have shown that high-valent Mn-dimers have reduction potentials similar to that of the tyrosyl radical in standard class I RNRs, but are hitherto not observed in RNRs (Roos and Siegbahn, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from prior computational work.

claim: High-valent Mn-dimers have not been observed in RNRs prior to this study.
source: Indeed, earlier calculations have shown that high-valent Mn-dimers have reduction potentials similar to that of the tyrosyl radical in standard class I RNRs, but are hitherto not observed in RNRs (Roos and Siegbahn, 2011).
evidence: This is stated as prior knowledge with citation.

claim: ITC binding curves for dATP, ATP and dADP to NrdB were all consistent with a single set of binding sites.
source: Binding curves for dATP, ATP and dADP to NrdB, including a reverse titration of NrdB to dATP, were all consistent with a single set of binding sites except for the ATP-cone deletion mutant (NrdBΔ99), which did not bind nucleotides at all (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments in Figure 8.

claim: The ATP-cone deletion mutant (NrdBΔ99) did not bind nucleotides at all.
source: Binding curves for dATP, ATP and dADP to NrdB, including a reverse titration of NrdB to dATP, were all consistent with a single set of binding sites except for the ATP-cone deletion mutant (NrdBΔ99), which did not bind nucleotides at all (Figure 8).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ITC experiments in Figure 8e.

claim: Using a fixed stoichiometry of 2, dATP binding to NrdB indicated 59% active (i.e. nucleotide binding) protein.
source: Using information available from the 3D structure, a fixed stoichiometry of 2 was used to fit dATP binding to NrdB. The fit indicated 59% active (i.e. nucleotide binding) protein.
evidence: This is calculated from ITC data fitting.

claim: Each NrdB monomer can bind two molecules of adenosine nucleotides.
source: Fitting dADP and ATP with a 59% proportion of active protein taken from the dATP experiment, we could calculate stoichiometries of 2.2 and 2.1 for ATP and dADP respectively, indicating that each NrdB monomer can bind two molecules of adenosine nucleotides (Figure 8f).
evidence: This is calculated from ITC data in Figure 8f.

claim: The Kd for ATP binding to NrdB is 38-fold lower affinity compared to dATP.
source: Kd for the three different nucleotides (Figure 8f) indicated a 38-fold and 15-fold lower affinity for ATP and dADP compared to dATP.
evidence: This is calculated from ITC data in Figure 8f.

claim: The Kd for dADP binding to NrdB is 15-fold lower affinity compared to dATP.
source: Kd for the three different nucleotides (Figure 8f) indicated a 38-fold and 15-fold lower affinity for ATP and dADP compared to dATP.
evidence: This is calculated from ITC data in Figure 8f.

claim: The interactions of nucleotides with the ATP-cone are enthalpy-driven, with negative ΔH values of −79, −44 and −103 for dATP, ATP and dADP respectively.
source: Thermodynamic parameters (Figure 8f) indicated that the interactions are enthalpy-driven, with negative ΔH values of −79,–44 and −103 for dATP, ATP and dADP respectively.
evidence: This is measured by ITC experiments in Figure 8f.

claim: This is the first observation of dADP binding to the ATP-cone of an RNR enzyme.
source: Structurally, binding of dADP is not surprising, since the γ-phosphates of the dATP molecules make only one interaction with the protein, through Arg102, and they only contribute 2 of the 6 coordinating atoms of the intervening Mg2+ ion. Nonetheless, this is the first observation of dADP binding to the ATP-cone of an RNR enzyme.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on ITC and structural data.

claim: The ATP-cone is an example of allosteric regulation controlled by a domain that acts relatively independent of the catalytic core of proteins.
source: The ATP-cone is an example of allosteric regulation controlled by a domain that acts relatively independent of the catalytic core of proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about ATP-cone function.

claim: Allosteric regulation controlled by ATP-cones can be lost or gained in RNRs through evolutionary time.
source: This type of allosteric regulation has been shown to provide an evolutionarily dynamic process by which allosteric regulation can be lost or gained both in RNRs (Lundin et al., 2015) and other enzymes (Aravind and Koonin, 1999; Lang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: The lack of activity regulation through an ATP-cone in the catalytic subunit is compensated by the presence of this domain in the non-homologous radical-generating subunit of some RNRs.
source: It hence appears as if the lack of activity regulation through an ATP-cone in the catalytic subunit is compensated by the presence of this domain in the non-homologous radical-generating subunit of some RNRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution of ATP-cones in different RNR subclasses.

claim: The ATP-cone does not require a long evolutionary period of integration with a protein to contribute to regulation.
source: This suggests that the ATP-cone, contrary to what might be expected for a domain involved in allostery, does not require a long evolutionary period of integration with a protein to contribute to regulation and that it hence lends itself to a highly dynamic evolution of allosteric activity control (Lundin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic distribution and functional data, supported by citation.

claim: No RNR in the phylogenetic subclass NrdAi/Bi contains an ATP-cone in the catalytic subunit.
source: No RNR in the phylogenetic subclass NrdAi/Bi contains an ATP-cone in the catalytic subunit, and only a minority – mostly encoded by Flavobacteriia, a marine class of Bacteroidetes – have an NrdB with an ATP-cone, suggesting the relatively recent acquisition of the ATP-cone to an RNR subclass that is otherwise not activity regulated (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1.

claim: Only a minority of NrdAi/Bi RNRs – mostly encoded by Flavobacteriia – have an NrdB with an ATP-cone.
source: No RNR in the phylogenetic subclass NrdAi/Bi contains an ATP-cone in the catalytic subunit, and only a minority – mostly encoded by Flavobacteriia, a marine class of Bacteroidetes – have an NrdB with an ATP-cone, suggesting the relatively recent acquisition of the ATP-cone to an RNR subclass that is otherwise not activity regulated (Figure 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1.

claim: The phylogenetic distribution suggests the relatively recent acquisition of the ATP-cone to the NrdAi/Bi RNR subclass.
source: No RNR in the phylogenetic subclass NrdAi/Bi contains an ATP-cone in the catalytic subunit, and only a minority – mostly encoded by Flavobacteriia, a marine class of Bacteroidetes – have an NrdB with an ATP-cone, suggesting the relatively recent acquisition of the ATP-cone to an RNR subclass that is otherwise not activity regulated (Figure 1).
evidence: This is inferred from phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1.

claim: The C-terminally positioned ATP-cone in the Ib subclass NrdF might be an example of an even more recent evolutionary event.
source: Moreover, in the Ib subclass, which also lacks ATP-cones in the catalytic subunit, we detected a C-terminally positioned ATP-cone in the radical-generating subunit. This was found in only two sequences from closely related organisms and might hence be an example of an even more recent evolutionary event.
evidence: This is inferred from the very limited phylogenetic distribution.

claim: ATP-cones could potentially be used to control the activity of engineered proteins.
source: The evidence we have presented here for an ATP/dATP-sensing master switch of the L. blandensis NrdAi/NrdBi class I RNR, suggests a potential for the use of ATP-cones to control the activity of engineered proteins.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings of the study.

claim: Multimeric enzymes could be inactivated through sequestration of one member of an active complex by control of dATP concentrations in the reaction mixture.
source: Multimeric enzymes could be inactivated through sequestration of one member of an active complex, by control of dATP concentrations in the reaction mixture.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential application based on the mechanism observed.

claim: The active center of the radical generating subunit of class I RNRs have been found to consist either of an FeIIIFeIII or MnIIIMnIII pair coupled to a tyrosine residue, or a FeIIIMnIV center not coupled to an amino acid radical.
source: The active center of the radical generating subunit of class I RNRs have earlier been found to consist either of an FeIIIFeIII or MnIIIMnIII pair coupled to a tyrosine residue acting as long-term storage for the catalytically essential radical (Berggren et al., 2017; Cotruvo and Stubbe, 2012), or a FeIIIMnIV center not coupled to an amino acid radical (Griese et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies.

claim: L. blandensis NrdBi appears to present a fourth type of metal center: a high-valent MnIIIMnIV center that lacks a suitably positioned radical storage amino acid.
source: Although further analyses are required to fully characterize the L. blandensis NrdBi active center, it appears to present a fourth type, a high-valent MnIIIMnIV center that lacks a suitably positioned radical storage amino acid.
evidence: This is inferred from EPR data and structural analysis.
